Warm-up: Everyone has arrived somewhere late. Four answers, then move on.
The hotel words arrive in Stage 2.
Vocabulary: Check in is the verb, check-in the noun. Same for check out / checkout. Say it once.
Is breakfast included? is the single most useful question in this lesson. Drill the intonation, not the grammar.
Grammar: Could you = you do it. Could I = I do it. That distinction is the whole stage.
In requests, please goes at the end far more often than at the front.
This is functional language, not grammar. Do not turn it into a paradigm.
Practice: Exercise 3 is about register, not about grammar. Students who say the direct version are not wrong in form, only in tone.
Exercise 5 brings back will, might and the indefinite pronouns from Lessons 19 and 20. Name it as recycling.
Listening: The first goes well, the second does not. Ask which one they would rather have.
Nine phrases in the speaker’s own voice. Play them again before the role play.
The model: They are not answering comprehension questions. They are looking for the parts they will reuse.
The note is polite and slightly formal. The message to a friend is not. That contrast is the point.
Now you: Each student sees only their own card. Do not let them read each other’s.
The second run is where the language is learned. Do not cut it for time.
One phrase used well, one to try next time.
Wrap: Will, might and the indefinite pronouns all came back today.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Asking for things without sounding rude

The same request, two words apart from an argument.

Read these four lines from the recording.
  • I’d like to check in, please.
  • Could you fill in the registration form, please?
  • Could I just check a couple of things about the room?
  • Is there somewhere we can leave our luggage?
In the second and third lines, who does the action?
What do you want to do?
What you wantThe phraseExample
You want them to do itCould you + verb…, please?Could you send someone up, please?
You want to do itCould I + verb…, please?Could I have a spare key, please?
You want somethingI’d like + noun / to + verbI’d like to check in, please.
You want to know if it existsIs there / Are there…?Is there a charge for it?
You want to know if you can use itIs … available?Is Wi-Fi available in the room?
You want a timeWhat time is…?What time is checkout?
Something is wrongThere’s a problem with…There’s a problem with the heating.
Where please goesat the end, before the question mark — Could you sign here, please? It can also open a request: Please could I…

THE CHOICE. Could you…? asks the other person to act. Could I…? asks for permission or for a thing. Both take the plain verb, with no to.

WHY IT MATTERS. Give me a spare key is correct English and sounds rude. Could I have a spare key, please? is the same request, politely.

The mistake to watch: Could you to send someone up? There is no to after could.

THE CHOICE. Could you…? asks the other person to do something: Could you send someone up? Could I…? asks for a thing or for permission: Could I have a spare key?

FORM. Could is followed by the plain verb, with no to and no -s: Could you send…, not Could you to send… or Could he sends…

SOFTENERS. Please usually goes at the end. Just makes a request smaller: Could I just check one thing? Possibly makes it more careful: Could you possibly bring me a towel?

REPLYING. Yes, of course. · Certainly. · I’m afraid not. · I’m afraid the room isn’t ready yet. The receptionist in the recording uses I’m afraid to give bad news gently.

Two mistakes to watch: Could you to help me? (no to), and using the bare imperative — Bring me a towel — which is grammatically fine and socially wrong.

You already know how to say what is possible: might, from Lesson 19, is what a receptionist uses when they cannot promise. The room might be ready by one.

Listen and read. Five phrases from the recording, one at a time.

Full grammar reference — Hotel language and polite requests

Form

ArrivingI’d like to check in, please. · I have a reservation under Samson.
AskingIs breakfast included? · What time do we have to check out?
Reporting a problemThere’s a problem with the heating. · The room is very cold.
RequestingCould you send someone up? · Would it be possible to change rooms?
Asking for one moreCould I have a spare towel, please?

When and why we use it

  • Could is more polite than can, and far more polite than the plain imperative.
  • Report a problem before you ask for the solution — the two-step order sounds reasonable, not aggressive.
  • Please goes at the end of the request, after a comma.
  • A written note keeps the same order: room number → problem → request → when you will be back.

Signal words

single / double room · reception · included · spare · extra · available

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I want a towel. → Could I have a towel, please?I want sounds rude in a service situation.
  • There is a problem of the heating. → There is a problem with the heating.Problem with.
  • Can you to send someone? → Could you send someone?No to after could.
  • I have reservation. → I have a reservation.Countable noun needs an article.

Don’t confuse it with

check in = arrive and register. check out = pay and leave. Both are two words as verbs.

Stage 6 · The model

The note you leave at reception

Nobody is at the desk, your room is cold, and you are going out. This is what you write.

Read the note. You are reading it as a writer, not as a student — look for the parts you can reuse.

A note left at reception

Dear Reception,

I’m in room 412. There’s a problem with the heating — it doesn’t work and the room is very cold.

Could you send someone up this afternoon, please? I’ll be out between two and four, so anyone can come in then.

Could I also have an extra blanket and a spare key? Nobody was at the desk when I came down.

Thank you very much.

Aidana Serik, room 412

Note. Written for this course as writing models. The hotel, the guests and the room numbers are invented.

And two messages to a friend, about the same day.
